results.draft_locus: The Forked Platform: When the Core Has Been Changed ¶3
results.quote: Adobe ships an Upgrade Compatibility Tool that checks a customized instance's modules and core code against a target version and reports "critical issues, errors, and warnings" (updated 8 October 2026).
results.finding: The paragraph states the tool's existence but no sentence says what it shows; the spec's 'shows' (a vendor building a tool for this is a sign of how common the problem is) is missing, so the evidence is left for the reader to interpret.

results.quote: the checkout template and Scripts it replaced were withdrawn on the dates given in the Forked Platform section above
results.finding: Both flow readers found the Shopify Functions/checkout template/Scripts timeline told a third time (Functions subsection, Pulled Rug paragraph, In Practice) and could not see why the dated vendor examples sit in In Practice; reader B calls their position unclear. The spec places this repeated case in p44 by design.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flowA: 'Dated public examples, first bullet: the Shopify Functions and Scripts timeline is told for the third time'

results.draft_locus: The Choices: Where Custom Behavior Should Live ¶1
results.quote: Pete Hodgson's 2017 taxonomy of feature toggles (switches that turn behavior on or off without a release) helps decide whether a switch is a release, ops or permissioning toggle, and so whether it belongs in configuration at all.
results.finding: Both readers stumbled on the Hodgson aside inside rung 1: the three toggle types are unexplained and the link to 'belongs in configuration' is unclear, pulling the reader off the ladder.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flowB: 'whether a switch is a release, ops or permissioning toggle: three terms left unexplained, in an aside that pulls away from the ladder'

results.draft_locus: The Forked Platform: When the Core Has Been Changed ¶6
results.quote: Hosted platforms cannot be forked, but they withdraw extension points, which is the same risk from the other direction; the book's name for it is **the Pulled Rug**.
results.finding: Both readers report that the section heading ('When the Core Has Been Changed') does not prepare them for the hosted deprecation risk it also covers; the spec deliberately joins the two risks in one section under that title.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flowA: 'a deprecation risk sits inside a section titled "When the Core Has Been Changed", so the section heading undersells what the section covers'

results.quote: The Secret Agent — an app that writes stock
results.finding: The opening failure-pattern box does not match the body: it names the Secret Agent and the Spaghetti Junction, which never recur (reader B kept waiting for them), and omits the Pulled Rug, which the body names twice (reader A).
results.corroborated_by: reader-flowA: 'The Pulled Rug is also missing from the opening failure-pattern box even though it gets a name here and in When It Goes Wrong'

results.draft_locus: Five Ways to Extend a Platform ¶12
results.quote: The five mechanisms meet in four interactions a merchant actually has.
results.finding: Reader A could not map the five mechanisms onto the four rows (theme code absent, functions and call-outs share a row, webhook added then called part of apps) and had to re-read the earlier table. The five-to-four framing comes from the spec's p22.

results.draft_locus: Five Ways to Extend a Platform ¶11
results.quote: **An extension point is a named moment with a fixed input, a fixed output, a time budget and a failure rule.**
results.finding: Reader B found two incompatible definitions of 'extension point': p13 makes all five mechanisms kinds of extension point, p21 defines it in terms that fit only functions and call-outs, leaving unclear whether a plugin is one. Both definitions are in the spec (p13, p21).

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Forty-One Apps and One Spreadsheet ¶3
results.quote: That feed is one chain: the **integration platform as a service (iPaaS)**
results.finding: Reader B lost the thread: ¶3 introduces the three apps then turns to describe the warehouse feed, and ¶4 ('One app copies stock adjustments…') returns to the three apps without signalling it, so the reader had to look back to see it was the list.

results.draft_locus: The Choices: Where Custom Behavior Should Live ¶1
results.quote: whether a switch is a release, ops or permissioning toggle
results.finding: Three toggle categories are used without explanation; they are not in already_knows and the draft never glosses them, and both flow readers reported them as unexplained.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flowA and reader-flowB both report the three toggle types as unexplained
